facts.statement: Ostromia fossils were recovered from the Late Jurassic Painten Formation in Germany and the genus was named by Christian Foth and Oliver Rauhut in 2017.
facts.quote: Recovered from the Late Jurassic Painten Formation of Germany, it was named by Christian Foth and Oliver Rauhut in 2017.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was discovered near Riedenburg, Germany, in 1855 and was originally misidentified as a pterosaur species named Pterodactylus crassipes in 1857.
facts.quote: The holotype (Teylers specimens TM 6928 and 6929) was discovered near Riedenburg, Germany in 1855 and it was originally misidentified as a species of a pterodactyloid pterosaur and named Pterodactylus crassipes in 1857.

facts.statement: In 1970, paleontologist John Ostrom identified the specimen as Archaeopteryx and named it the "Haarlem specimen" because it was housed in the Teylers Museum in Haarlem.
facts.quote: In 1970 it was identified as an Archaeopteryx by paleontologist John Ostrom, who called it the "Haarlem specimen", since it was kept in the Teylers Museum in Haarlem.

facts.statement: In 2017, Christian Foth and Oliver Rauhut reclassified the specimen as a new genus named Ostromia, honoring John Ostrom, after concluding it was more closely related to Anchiornis.
facts.quote: In 2017 Christian Foth and Oliver Rauhut concluded it was more closely related to the Chinese Anchiornis and introduced the generic name Ostromia, named after Ostrom.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Ostromia is incomplete, preserving only limb bones, cervical vertebrae, and ribs.
facts.quote: The only known specimen is fairly incomplete compared to most specimens of Archaeopteryx, as it only preserves limb bones, cervical vertebrae and ribs.

facts.statement: Ostromia has a larger length ratio between the third and first metacarpals of the hand compared to any Archaeopteryx specimen.
facts.quote: The length ratio between the third and the first metacarpal of the hand is larger in Ostromia than in any Archaeopteryx specimen.

facts.statement: In Ostromia, the claw of the first hand digit is smaller than the corresponding metacarpal, whereas in Archaeopteryx the claw is larger.
facts.quote: In addition, the ungual (claw) of the first digit of the hand is smaller than the corresponding first metacarpal, while in Archaeopteryx the claw is larger.

facts.statement: The pubic bone of Ostromia is strongly flexed backwards with a triangular boot, a feature similar to Anchiornis but unlike Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: The pubic shaft of the Haarlem specimen is also strongly flexed backwards and has a triangular pubic boot, similar to the pubis of Anchiornis but unlike that of Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: Foth and Rauhut (2017) classified Ostromia within the family Anchiornithidae as the only known European member.
facts.quote: Foth and Rauhut (2017) recovered Ostromia within Anchiornithidae as the only known European member of this family.

facts.statement: Agnolin et al. (2019) debated that Ostromia should be considered an indeterminate paravian rather than an anchiornithid, citing similarities to Unenlagiinae.
facts.quote: Agnolin et al. (2019) argued that the putative anchiornithid affinities of Ostromia are also seen in Unenlagiinae, and that it is best to consider this genus as an indeterminate paravian.

facts.statement: Recent studies, including work by Mulder et al. (2024), suggest that micro-CT analysis may provide a definitive solution to the ongoing debate over Ostromia's classification.
facts.quote: Other recent work on the genus further discusses its position within Anchiornithidae, including work by Mulder et al. (2024) which hints at micro-CT analysis of the fossil that should provide a definitive solution to its classification.

facts.statement: A 2026 study by O'Connor & Marugán-Lobón argued that the diagnostic characters of Ostromia are equivocal and the fossil likely represents Archaeopteryx, while a subsequent 2026 revision by Foth & Rauhut interpreted it as an indeterminate avialan.
facts.quote: O'Connor & Marugán-Lobón (2026) revise the fossil record of avialans from the Upper Jurassic Solnhofen Limestones (Germany), consider purported diagnostic characters of Ostromia crassipes and Alcmonavis poeschli to be equivocal, and interpret the studied fossils as most likely representing a single taxon (Archaeopteryx); another revision of Solnhofen avialans is subsequently published by Foth & Rauhut (2026), who interpret the holotype of Ostromia crassipes as an indeterminate avialan, and interpret Alcmonavis poeschli as likely to be a distinct taxon.

facts.statement: Ostromia lived during the Late Jurassic, specifically the Kimmeridgian stage, in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente entre a millones de años, durante el Kimmeridgiense, en lo que es hoy Europa.
